Article III Of the new covenant provides:

Phrase Not Defined

Several Instances Cited

June 10, 1846—President Polk submitted to the Senate for its advice the incomplete treaty with Great Britain on the Oregon boundary; it was formally approved by the Senate, concluded by the President, approved in its final form by the Senate and ratified, all within nine days.

With his installation in st. Pat
rick's Cathedral the Most Rev
Patrick j. Hayes became the
Archbishop of New York, entitled tc
wear the ermine cappa magma and
the lambs wool pallium, and tC
exercise the functions of supreme
spiritual director of the clergy and
faithful of the great Archdiocese Of
New York. The ceremony of in.
stallation, conducted by the Apos-
tolic Delegate, Archbishop John
Bonzano, was an admixture of an
cient rites and symbols, which are
a part of the church itself, and oil
modern thought and practice. The
presence of a host of priests in the
military uniforms of chaplains OF
army and navy in itself gave a most
unusual touch to the entire picture
and mingled oddly in the pageantry
Of the white satin of the two Arch
bishops, the purplish red of the
Monsignori, the dull gray and brown
robes of the friars, and the black
cassocks and white SUPPLIES of the
simple priests.


The occasion was chosen by Arch
bishop Bonzano as a fitting one on
which to express the church view
on the present critical condition in
world affairs. Most diplomats make
such utterances at banquets, usually
arranged for that specific purpose,
but the installation of the new
Archbishop of New York gave the
Papal diplomat the opportunity, for
- ~, hfc ~ DID ~ a
to Archbishop Hayes when he be-
gan to recount the conditions the
exalted prelate would find facing
him.


Archbishop Hayes" he said, "be-
gins his administration at mo-
ment that is critical for America
and for all mankind. In every de-
partment of life problems of the
gravest character multiply day by
day. Still trembling from it's
mighty conflict, the world is Inn
patient to clear away its ruins and
build anew the structure of society.
Law and order, individual right and
national existence, science and civ
llization-all are involved in this
crisis. Religion itself is not exempt,
nor faith, nor hope, nor the vir-
tues that have hitherto served as
the basis of freedom-all are at
stake, all dependent upon the issue
to which events are so rapidly NOV
ing. 1t is plainly seen that the
world has to learn new lesson, or
to learn again what it has so long
forgotten. After trying its own
wisdom and finding it failure the
world must go back to the wisdom
of Christ and his gospel. In the
solution of these grave problems,
America will have her full share of
opportunity, and likewise OF respon-
sibility. According to the measure
of her wisdom in this crisis will be
the weight of her influence for good
upon all other nations"


Archbishop Hayes in his response
touched, upon world matters, and
fervently proclaimed that the sue
cess of the Peace Conference de-
pended upon the spirit of Christian
ity in which it was conducted, and
the extent to which the teachings OF
Christ govern it's decisions and con-
illusions.


While the Pope was in no haste
in promulgating the appointment OF
the new Archbishop he expedited
matters to have the new Metropoli-
tan take actual charge of his see.
Aside from the Importance OF hav-
ing O permanent head to the great
archdiocese, there was a church
reason for the hurry. 1t is a law
of the Catholic church that an
nointing oils used in various rites,
such as baptism, ordination and ex-
treme JUNCTION, must be not over a
year old, the church year being
measured from Easter to Easter. 1t
is at Easter time these oils are
blessed, and they must be blessed
by an Archbishop. Therefore 1t Is
a necessity If the clergy are to have
these oils for the ensuing year that
there shall be an Archbishop to
bless them before sEaster. Hence
the special haste in investing Arch
bishop Hayes with the full author
ity of his office.


The ceremony of installation was
an informal one. The main feature
was the act Of obedience on the part
Of the clergy, who will thus pledge
their fealty to the new Metropoli-
tan.


This ceremony invested the new
Archbishop with the full power Of
his office, though his investiture will
not be complete until the imposition
of the pallium. The pallium is a
cape which goes on over the head
and rests on both shoulders. 1t is
made of wool shorn from lambs
raised on the Vatican grounds, and
woven into fabric by the Sisters
Of st. Agnes in Rome. Symbolically,
the pallium means that the Arch
bishop is proclaimed lamb Of God.

To my mind, the first step in this direction, assuming that Congress approves the general plan, is to secure a body of land of sufficient size in the District of Columbia, adjoining the city of Washington, to accommodate the largest possible collection of buildings for a permanent world's exposition. No less than 1,000 acres, a tract 5,000 feet on a side, would be suitable for the final and logical development of the idea, although the buildings might be few at first. Get the land, dedicate it to the purpose, and see how quickly not only our own, but the people of other lands will enthusiastically support it. In fact, through a system of charges for exhibition space and contributions, the cost of the land itself might be returned to our treasury, and that of the buildings and exhibits and running expenses met the same way. Within a few years the whole exposition should be self-supporting, and of such intrinsic value to all concerned as to pay for itself many times over, if only from a social, scientific and humanitarian point of view.

What is more natural than to look for a clearing house of nations to follow the establishment of a League of Nations? And if America was foremost in bringing about this great league, has she not the first right to the clearing house, especially as she can deliver the goods? And if there is to be a clearing house of nations, where can it be placed if not in the capital city of the country where the league of all men had its rise? Placed at Washington, it will have a distinct international importance, which no one would attach to it if it were established in any other city in America. No other city has the room for it, nowhere else will it be as a city set upon a hill for the eyes of all men to turn to it, as in Washington.

Let the advocates of a permanent national exposition go ahead and keep their project alive; it all works in the same direction. But let no one think that one or half a dozen buildings set down in the heart of the city will suffice. Let all work for the larger site. A few words as to how far this idea has gone will be interesting.

Other Cities Want Exposition.

Since The Star, in February, 1907, outlined the idea of a permanent world's exposition at Washington, Brazil and Uruguay have opened prospective capitals. The Hague, capital of Holland, has plans for a permanent world exposition, as shown by consular reports. Constant rumors are heard in New York of plans for something of the kind here, and about a year ago a permanent exposition was opened in the Bronx, covering a large tract.

The results have fully justified my contention from the beginning, that neither New York nor any other city but Washington can be regarded as the proper site for an enterprise of such worldwide significance as this. It may be added that a French enthusiast named Anderson published a very expansive book some years ago containing full plans for a world capitol to be located in the United States, and copies of this work were deposited with the heads of all governments. Mr. Anderson is wishing to locate his capitol at Lakewood, N. J. He is said to have spent $2,000,000 in boosting this idea; we have seen none of his plans that were made prior to the publication of similar plans in The Star.

While reconstruction is proceeding, plans should be made for an exposition of our states, and the plan of inviting Latin America to participate should be carefully studied. A large part of the 5,000-acre tract should be set apart for pleasing to our neighbors to the south and valuable to both sides. In 1914 Brazil was planning to negotiate for a space for a Brazilian building at Washington, but the war stopped it all.

The vast and growing interests of this country alone demand big space for exhibition, and we are in our youth yet. Commercial solidarity will make for lasting peace. It is worth all it will cost.

was to me that he presented his let-
ter of appointment. All the young
men did. Then I had to line them
up and march them to barracks."

"What do I remember about Gen-
eral Pershing—Jack? Not much.
He was as the other boys who re-
ported that day as the boys who had
reported before him, and as the boys
who have reported since—a fine,
clean, outstanding young man,
worthy of West Point and of West
Point traditions."

Pershing Becomes Beast.

Barracks" to which old Woods
marched Jack Pershing, was then,
and is today, known as "Beast Bar-
racks." And the cadets marched
there are known as "Beasts," a de-
gree lower in the cadet hierarchy
than Plebes. There followed the
usual program for Jack Pershing.
He deposited with the proper off-
icals the small sum of money re-
quired by government regulations
and with it all the jewelry and valu-
ables he carried.

Government regulations prescribe
the amount of money they shall
have to spend—50 cents a week, as
I recall it—and the amount of
money they shall be paid. Which
amount, however, is not paid until
they are graduated. Each boy has
the same chance. A true democracy
is West Point—giving much, de-
manding much.

Oh, the commands of that break-
ing in" period, snapped out by stern
drill masters, yearling corporals,
who act under the direction of for-
mer cadets, now officers in the army
and back under special orders to
serve for a time as tactical in-
structors, or "Tacs," as the cadets
call them in their own slang.

Fall IN!

"Fall out!"

"Hold up your head!"
"Drag in your chin!"
"Suck up your stomach!"
"Get those shoulders back! More
yet! More yet!"

Lordly Young Men.

How those Yearling corporals
could yell and did yell at "Beasts."
And if one forgot to salute those
lordly young men or the "TAGS," or
forgot to address them as "Sir,"
Oh, those "Beast" days! Especial-
ly the days when that most high-
est of all, commander even of the
"TAGS," the Commandant of Cadets
and Tactical Officers, put in appear-
ance! Why, it was even prescribed
how cadets should sit at mess!
There was no end of regulations.
Rooms must be kept just SO; beds
must be made just SO; bedding must
be kept just so; equipment, all of
it, must be kept just so; everything
must be kept just so. An inch out
of the way, a shoe or a paper mis-
placed, and—woe to the offender!
Camp lasted until September,
camp with all that the name im-
plied. It meant sleeping in the
open, Misunderstanding drills,
guard duty, swimming, dancing.
Oh, the fun of it and the work of
it! The trouble was then, even as
today, the Plebes were always the
butt of the fun.

Will Jack Pershing ever forget
the first time he heard the order:
"Chase the Eagles!"
"Turn out, YOU Plebes, and chase
those eagles!"

What did it mean? An unoffend-
ing, chirping sparrow had alighted
in company street, between rows
of tents. Poor sparrow! He was a
trespasser and must be ejected.
So the Plebes chased eagles.
Or did Jack Pershing forget an-
other order:

"Pick up those logs of wood, you
Plebes!"

The Funeral Of a Rat.

What did it mean! Someone
had thrown matches in the company
street. The Plebes must pick them
up. Yes, most of the police duty
fell to the lot of the Plebes. And
the tasks they had to do for upper
classmen. For West Point, in the
days of Jack Pershing, boosted that
English school system of "Tagging."
How the yearlings and the second
class and first-class men did all
within their power to make guard
duty for Plebes memorable.
Jack Pershing walked his post.
Out of the darkness of the night
would appear a number of white
wrapped forms—suspiciously like
cadets with sheets draped about
them.

"Who goes there?" the sentry
would cry.

"A flock of angels" would come.

In the whole world, there is no community of the same size that did more to help win the war than the Borough of Penns Grove, and its neighbor, Carney's Point.

Like every other patriotic community, we sent our full quota of men to the front and because of conditions here, perhaps more than a full quota. Penns Grove and Carney's Point sent 751 men to fight in the World War. The boys who went from our own school were: Oscar Hunt, Fred Craig, Frank Diver, Powell Craig, Ernest Johnson, VanDyke Conover, Edwin Bennett, Joseph Hendrickson, Earl Slape, Paul Kidd, Evan Walker, Samuel Turner, Joseph Straughn, Belford Wood, Fred McGee, Frank Denny, Max and Charles Bodine, James Smith, Willard Claire, Harold Huber, Raymond and Edward Hurley. Of this number Evan Walker made the supreme sacrifice, as you all know. The men that Penns Grove sent out to fight the battles of our country did their full duty. They brought great glory and credit to the State. They upheld the glorious traditions of America and gave us an honor roll which is second to none. New Jersey, although one of the smallest States in the area, stands among the first ten in the number of men who responded to the call of duty.

Every Red Cross movement was helped. In the two Red Cross enrollment drives approximately $4,000 was raised with a membership of about 10000. The Red Cross work rooms were always occupied. They furnished more than 1000 surgical dressings and hospital supplies, 1900 knitted garments, 470 comfort kits and other articles, besides the clothing sent for the Belgians. Magazines and books were collected and shipped to our soldiers at cantonments and abroad. First-aid classes were organized under Dr. Fleming, Mrs. Stocks and Miss Bingham. Now a course of vocational training is offered to the returned soldiers.

Every campaign for raising funds for the boys in the service was given our full support. Penns Grove's financial assistance in the war always kept it in the forefront of the communities having the highest percentage of contributions.

The Women's Club of Penns Grove and the Mothers Club of Carney's Point did their bit by helping in the Third, Fourth and Fifth Liberty Loans, and in the other drives, such as War Savings Stamps, Red Cross Enrollment, the two War Relief Drives, and in the food conservation campaign. The records of any of the other organizations would show just as loyal devotion.

Every Liberty Loan campaign was greatly over-subscribed. In our first Liberty Loan we raised about $100,000; in the second, $51,000; in the third we received our Honor Flag, containing two bars, signifying we had gone over the top in our loan twice. In the Fourth Loan we raised about $350,000. In the Victory Loan, which was to bring our boys home, we raised $500,050. Our sum total of all loans was approximately $1,000,900. What a glorious success all our loans were!

Besides our money and men we have other sources of pride. We not only sent the boys out to fight the Hun, but we also made the powder that they used. Penns Grove's contribution to the war in an industrial sense was one of the greatest of any community in the world no matter what its size. The great powder factory at Carney's Point was one of the most vital factors in winning the great victory. We can take great pride in this factory because every family did something to make this great war a success.

Our community, like other communities, was in the war for four years. We knew what it was to have thousands of men coming here to take part in making munitions. Thousands of men learned how to make powder here. The result was that our community not only made more smokeless powder than any other community in the United States, but trained more powder makers, who were able, when the time came, to go from here and man other powder factories to help increase the output of munitions.

Let us consider for a few moments what this great powder plant has done towards winning the war. We are justified in doing this because the powder plant is a part of Penns Grove's life and many of our boys who afterwards joined the colors had already done their part in making munitions in this plant.

The great powder plant at Carney's Point was for a long time the largest factory of its kind in supplying munitions to the European army. Vice President Taylor presided.

The committee does not believe that there was any intentional wrongdoing on the part of any one connected with the affair, but not one satisfied with the financial report of the program in charge, desires to make it known that the association does not countenance irregularities of any sort. The board of directors of the Arlington Trust Company at a meeting last night refused to accept the resignation of its president, W. W. Douglas, which was rendered several weeks ago. 900 Tons to Guard Commerce estimated for 1920.

Shipbuilding facilities acquired during the war have made the United States the greatest potential maritime power of the world, asserts Chairman E. N. Hurley of the shipping board, and will enable it to outdistance all other nations in the race toward replacing a shortage of 16,225,000 gross tons of shipping lost as the result of unrestricted German submarine warfare and of the failure of normal increase by new production. Mr. Hurley made this assertion in report of his trip to Europe, where for three months he was in close touch with the shipping interests of foreign nations. The report will be used in working out a policy of ownership and operation of the American merchant marine.

Mr. Hurley estimated that in July, 1914, the seagoing steam bottoms of the world totaled 41,225,000 gross tons, which was reduced by war to 37,000,000 gross tons, a net loss of 4,225,000 gross tons. In addition, he stated, there was a loss of 12,000,000 gross tons which would have been constructed if war had not stopped the normal increase in production, making a total loss of 16,225,000 gross tons. The allies and neutrals suffered a total loss by enemy action, marine risk, and capture of 15,474,000 gross tons, Mr. Hurley said, and gained by new construction and seizure of enemy ships 14,249,000 gross tons, leaving a net loss of 1,225,000 gross tons. The net loss to the central powers was even greater, since they lost 3,016,000 gross tons and gained only 740,000, a difference of 2,276,000 gross tons.

United States Takes Lead.
Only two countries, the United States and Japan, have a larger amount of tonnage now than when the war began. Japan showed a net gain of 5 per cent, Mr. Hurley reported, while the United States jumped far in the lead with a net gain of 125 per cent.

"The United States forged ahead as rapidly as Germany fell behind" said the report. In August, 1914, the United States seagoing merchant marine, 800 gross tons and over, included 624 steamers of 1,755,465 gross tons, and 40 sailing vessels and schooner barges of 7,852 gross tons, making a grand total of 664 seagoing merchant vessels of 1,763,317 gross tons. On November 11, 1918, at the end of the war, the steamgoing merchant marine had increased to 1886 vessels of 4,655,263 gross tons and the sailing vessels and schooner barges had decreased to 74 vessels of 780,917 gross tons, making a grand total of 2,113 seagoing merchant vessels of 5,515,180 gross tons. This does not include the seized enemy vessels, which at the end of the war aggregated 81 vessels of 582,005 gross tons, of which number 81 of 546,210 gross tons were steamers and seven of 35,795 gross tons were sailing vessels.

The total construction in the United States added to the merchant marine during the war amounted to 575 vessels of 2,941,845 gross tons. The purchase from aliens of 233 vessels of 533,554 gross tons, the movement from the great lakes to the ocean of 66 steamers of 139,469 gross tons, and miscellaneous acquisitions amounting to 81 vessels of 39,219 gross tons are other sources of acquisition. The loss of 14 vessels of 322,214 gross tons by enemy action, of 275 vessels of 405,400 gross tons by marine risk, of 130 vessels of 265,149 gross tons by sale to aliens, and of 14 vessels of 1,927 gross tons through the sale to the United States government, abandonment and other causes, accounts for the decreases. Losses of fifteen German and requisitioned ships amounting to 112,245 gross tons are not included.

"To-day we are potentially the greatest maritime power of the earth, for the reason that we possess the greatest shipbuilding instrumentalities."

All Try to Come Back.

Mr. Hurley stated that Great Britain suffered a net loss in the war of 5,443,000 gross tons, amounting to 15 per cent of her entire tonnage. The balance taken August 5 indicated that the balance had dwindled down to $21. He sold the twenty-nine lots he owned near Twenty-seventh and Iowa streets a few days ago to C. J. Bressler, 1885 Lime street, for $500 cash, and it is presumed this money was turned over to owners of a tract of land near Shorey which it is known Gordon contemplated purchasing.

Rusty Gun Near Body.
A rusty .32 caliber revolver was found by his side. The position of his body when it was discovered by Bressler this morning, together with the peculiar position that the revolver was found in caused the first suspicion of foul play. The bullet plowed thru the right temple and out the left. Gordon's hands were folded across his abdomen. The revolver was tucked, barrel down, under his left arm pit.

It was known that Sunday night Gordon sold a colt to L. E. Kidney, who lives near Twenty-sixth street and California avenue, probably a block from the Gordon barn. Kidney was working at the Tom Doran farm a mile distant.

Loved His Mare.
When Kidney was interviewed, he stated that Gordon had offered to give him the colt if he would kill a mare which Gordon owned and which he seemed to be very fond of and wished to have killed before he moved. Kidney said he shot the mare about 10 o'clock Sunday night and buried it half a block from Gordon's barn. "After I killed the mare, Gordon lay down by her head for fully fifteen minutes," said Kidney. "Then after we dug a pit to bury the animal in it and the animal rolled into the pit, Gordon crawled down there and lay by the animal's head."

Kidney stated that Coffman left early and he and Gordon worked until 2 o'clock in the morning burying the mare. Neighbors all stated that Gordon had grieved over being obliged to part with the mare which he said his father had given him eighteen years ago and had been his companion ever since.

"He asked me for it and I refused to give it to him. Gordon then pulled his gun out of his pocket. It was old and rusty. Kidney shot the mare with Gordon's gun."

The revolver found by Gordon's side this morning tallies in every way with the description of the revolver given by Coffman. The revolver when found this morning had only one ex.

His Room in Order.

Search of the little room which Gordon used as living and sleeping quarters revealed everything in order. There was $40 and some small change in a purse in his pocket. Coroner Narcotic stated that an inquest will be held in a few days after a more thorough investigation is made.

A Man of Mystery and Means.

Three years ago Gordon came to Topeka. He was about 35 years of age. He purchased twenty-nine lots in Highland Park and built a barn. In one section of the barn his horse, a mare, was stabled. In the other section he fitted out a bedroom for himself.

He became a favorite with the neighbors and the neighborhood children immediately after his arrival. ing cheers greeting the popular Admiral

Good old David" shouted the sub

enough war, enough peace, and now
want just regular navy life


London dropped it's dignity and

night it is happy, though hungry, tired

Learning to cook foods properly is an art. Also, learning when to stop cooking some foods is one of the important phases of this art. In general there are more foods spoiled by overlooking than by undercooking.

The finest example of this overcooking of foods is on display right now this season, when the gardens and the stores have ready for us all the lovely, new tender green peas that we can gather or afford to buy. But in more than half the cases the poor things are not allowed to make even half a showing—in other words, they are not given a square deal by the majority of women who cook and serve them.

Must Be Cooked Right.
When properly cooked there is not one person who will say but that new peas fresh from the vines are the most delightful vegetable grown.

It is quite commonly said by persons commenting upon the subject, that they would as soon have canned peas as the fresh ones. And in defense of the new peas, I want to say that the person who makes that statement may be honest in doing so, but he lacks the experience to make comparisons; he has never tasted new, fresh peas served under the conditions which offer them at their best.

In general they are overlooked. In this respect they resemble eggs. The longer you cook them the harder they get. Peas also lose in flavor by prolonged cooking. Much of this flavor will pass off in the steam; in some cases, I have known, they have been cooked in great amount of water and then this water was drained off and thrown away.

Is it any wonder that the persons who have never tasted peas cooked any other way, prefer the canned ones?

Like oysters, peas are best cooked only until the surface shows signs of wrinkling or shriveling—but not until they resemble a cold baked apple. The size of the peas will regulate the length of time it takes. For some of the tiny sugar peas it will take only a few minutes, but for the large ones it may take ten or fifteen minutes.

Best Cooking Method.

Steamed in a small amount of water under a tight cover will cook them so the very best is retained. For some, the addition of salt and butter or salt and sweet cream is as much as is needed. But many prefer to have them creamed. If so, this method will be most satisfactory.

1 cup shelled peas, selected.
1 cup milk.
4 tablespoons butter.
2 tablespoons flour.
Salt.

Blend the butter and the flour, add the milk and cook over hot water until thick and smooth. Add the peas and when thoroughly mixed with the sauce, cover tightly and place the vessel in boiling water where it may cook until the peas show signs of wrinkling. It may take anywhere from ten to twenty minutes, but the peas should be served as soon as cooked. By this method all of the juice and the flavor are kept in the sauce.

Often new potatoes are added to peas and sauce, but this should not be done until the potatoes have been cooked and skinned.

I have known of women who cook peas and potatoes together, the entire time it took to cook the potatoes. They scraped the new potatoes, shelled the peas, and put them on together in a kettle of boiling water and cooked them whole until the potatoes were done sufficiently—drained this water, which contained the best of the vegetables, in the sink, made a paste of flour and water or milk, poured it over the peas and potatoes, added a lump of butter, then returned the kettle to the fire and cooked it all ten or fifteen minutes longer.

Why Taste Tells.

Some one else says, "I can't see why some pay so much over new peas—they don't taste any different from the canned ones." "I can see."

investigation of the lynching here
yesterday of Jay Lynch after he had
been sentenced to life imprisonment
for the murder of Sheriff John N. J.
Harlow, and the sheriff's 15-year-old
son, was begun at a conference today
between Prosecuting Attorney N. W.
Timmonds and Sheriff W. A. Seward

hanging and every effort made to
apprehend those who had a hand in

The advisability of asking Judge

investigation was being considered by
noon. They were somewhat doubtful
if the court has authority to call a
special grand jury. Prosecutor Timmonds being unable thus far to find

a move.

such judicial circuits as Barton county
is situated a special term of court and

Sheriff Seward and his assistants as

warrants had been issued. The coroner's jury late last night returned a

the elm tree upon which he was

Lynch failed. Stunned by being struck

which had first seized him, the unconscious man was placed under the tree

The branch, however, was too frail
and the body pitched downward.

a stronger branch was selected, the

Lynch's Body Buried.

Joplin, May 29.—At the office of a
undertaker shortly after noon
it was announced that the body of Jay
Lynch, who was hanged by a mob at
Lamar yesterday, had been taken to
Forest Park cemetery and buried.
A reporter who went to the cemetery
at 2 o'clock this afternoon reports
that the body is not at the cemetery
and after a long search of the territory surrounding the cemetery the reporter failed to find either the relatives or the casket containing Lynch's
body.

The grave digger at the cemetery
said he understood the grave he was
digging was to hold the Lynch body.
There is a suspicion that the announcement that Lynch had been
buried at Forest Park was a hoax, that the body is elsewhere.

Mr. Burns recently purchased the fifty-foot lot adjoining his present location on East State St., and is putting up a building which promises to be one of the best equipped morgues and undertaking parlors in the district. Berlin Saturday, Dec. 13.—(By The A. P.) In her note replying to the last entente communication demanding the signing of the protocol preliminary to putting the peace treaty in effect, which is now on its way to Paris, Germany yields in her stand on the Scapa Flow issue to a certain extent.

The text of the reply was handed on Friday night to a courier who at once started with it for the French capital. The text will not be published in Berlin before Monday.

It is learned that in the note Germany reiterates its desire to have ratification of the peace treaty effected at the earliest possible date. It gently hints that the entente is responsible for the complications which have delayed the exchange of ratifications for more than a month. It declares that Germany has not and is not now making the final ratification dependent upon the clauses relating to war prisoners or the extradition of German subjects for trial, although it expresses the hope that the allies will permit themselves to be convinced that both issues have an important bearing upon the internal political situation in Germany.

On the Scapa Flow issue the note expresses a willingness to yield to the extent that Germany will consent to make reparation for the sinking of the German warships, in order to remove what is characterized as the final obstacle to the definite conclusion of peace, although, says the note, reparation cannot be made in the manner suggested in the demand for 400,000 tons of shipping. On this point Germany proposes negotiations by the entente with a board of German shipping experts.

The note declares that the prospective temporary absence of Americans from the commissions established under the treaty has not influenced the attitude of official Germany towards the question of final ratification.

Your letter was received Feb. IA


and / was glad to hear from you all


again Wei; this letter leaves me


we'll now and hope to find you all


well when it reaches you. Well we


have been having some flu in the com


pany and some pneumonia. Also and


has killed some of the boys in the last


couple weeks but 1 thank the good


Lord for the good health that have


had since left the States. for hovent


answered but two sick calls yet and


I nithankfuI for that and thank the


Lord to give me strength and good


health till I reach home again. Well


T am sure that there are not very
many of the boys that made the trip
ny quicker than the fifty-fourth did
for we crossed the sea on Aug. 29th.
and landed on Sept. 18th A little
more than two weekh we were on the
front of Verdun There we started
to work and believe me we did some
work there The Fritzies shelled us
some but we didn't think that they
were going to hit us any way but some


of the shells burst in fifty yards from
where we were working. Trying to
hit the bridges that we were finishing
and we Were. close enough to see al
most the front line trenches. If there


hadn't been woods between us and


we dug in the hill side TO keep them


from picking US off. =.

war and I'm proud Of my experience
of warfareand the country that have


seen. 1 saw some of France that
was swept cleaner than any OF the
fields in the states and ] wah in the
Argonne forest and there was some
fighting done here. These woods
were torn to pieces. Oats two feet in
diameter We're cut off by the big shells
and we spent six weeks on tbis front.
From your son


Daniel F Price

The United States Government, after an extensive study, has decided that it will principally propose to write off millions from the cost of American shipping. "Inasmuch as one of the very important factors in ship operating costs is that part of the overhead cost represented by interest and depreciation, it is recognized that a readjustment of ship values should be made. the right to organize voluntarily and
the duty to submit to organization involuntarily. If the right of the fed.
Grafton should be conceded to organize any trade at its choice and without invitation, there would be an end
to the company union, whose right
and utility or humanity, it may be
added—is equal to the federation's.
This ground was fought even earlier
than the issues above discussed, and
was decided once for all early in this
century, in Roosevelt's time. This
is matter of citizens' rights, not of
humanity nor of unions' rights.

LONDON, June 8.—(3 P. M.)
—The German national assembly sitting at Weimar, is reported to have decided to sign the peace treaty though the terms have been submitted to the peace committee of the assembly for formal action.

This decision, it was reported, was taken following the resignation of the Scheidemann cabinet, which announced its decision to quit office at 1 o'clock this morning, following a lengthy session with the German peace delegation. — News of the downfall of the Scheidemann ministry reached London in dispatches from The Hague and later in reports from Paris. It is reported in peace conference circles at Paris that War Minister Gustave Noske, an avowed advocate of signing the treaty, will head the new German cabinet. This report is not officially confirmed.

The report that the national assembly has decided to sign came by exchange Telegraph dispatch from Paris, quoting advices from Weimar. This report was generally believed here in view of the resignation of the Scheidemann ministry, though it lacked official confirmation.

Four-fifths of the Zentrum party controlling eighty-eight of the votes in the national assembly, voted in favor of signing the treaty. The democrats voted fifty-six to nine against acceptance.

The Scheidemann ministry will continue to carry on the duties of the government until the new ministry is formed, said another exchange dispatch from Paris. Scheidemann and Foreign Minister von Brockdorff-Rantau had committed themselves too far against acceptance of the treaty to remain in office, the dispatch said.

Earlier dispatches from Vienna today had corroborated International News Service dispatches of yesterday from Weimar, showing a majority of the cabinet favored signing.

Following closely after the recent
burglary of the w. S. Huntley residence
on South Main street, the adjacent
neighborhood of South street had its
chapter of criminal mystery last Sat
urday forenoon. Mrs. Sophie A.
Knight, 81 years old of New York City,
who with her daughter, Anita, has been
boarding this summer at the home of


Mr. and Mrs. Solomon B. Aines on
South street, had been making it her
almost daily custom to visit the fields
at the extremity Of South street, where
she enjoyed the fine view of the Green
Mountains and usually fingered to read
or write The particular spot was the
knoll where the new Porter hospital
is to be built.


Last Saturday morning she was walk
ing to her favorite resting place in
this field when, as she passed Porter
Field, she noticed a strange man walk
ing toward the same field for which she
was bound. He wore a dark suit, a
soft gray hat, appeared to be about
80 years old, and was smooth shaven.
He had a reddish face, and carried a
small grip similar to a doctors bag.
Mrs Knight felt no alarm when she
saw him crossing into the field, as she
thought he was some workman having
business in the vicinity, and according
ly she went as usual to a nearby ledge
to write some letters and to eat an
orange which she carried in a handbag
for her refreshment. A little later while
she was peeling the orange with a pen
knife and enjoying the mountain view
20 the east, the man she had seen short
ly before jumped out from a clump of
bushes back of the spot where she was
sitting and grabbed her by the throat
making an ugly effort to strangle her.
She was unable to scream, but as there
was no house within hearing distance,
that was futile anyway, and she real
lied that she must defend herself. With
the pen knife which she had in her
hand she struck frantcally at the mans
face, cutting him badly near the eyes
and nose. In any event, the treatment
frightened him, and releasing his hold
on her throat he grabbed her hand bag,
which held little money and a gold
watch. and ran toward the Otter Creek.


Mrs. Knight although cut about her
own face by the rufian's finger nails
and bleeding considerably, still kept
her nerve and made all possible haste
to get back to her boarding place and
to notify the authorities. Sheriffs N.
]. Sanford and Edward Higgins were
quickly on the track of the man and
followed him by means of foot steps
along the river edge to a point near
the Three Mile bridge where the trail
was lost in swamp. A number of
others participated in the search and
kept at it relentlessly until there seemed
no possible chance of success, and the
telephoning OF the description of the
man to other places was equally futile.

They entered singly wearing dainty organdie frocks and carrying baskets of shasta daisies, the handles beautified with white tulle. Bands of tulle with touches of daisies encircled the little girls' heads and terminated in the back in a fluffy bow.

The little ring bearer was Master Albert Brady, Jr., the 2-year-old son of Mr. and Mrs. Albert Brady. He wore a suit of white linen and carried the ring embedded in rose.

The bride and groom entered together and were joined in marriage by Rev. H. Henderson, pastor of the church. The bride was lovely wearing a handsome suit of sand-colored poplin, exquisitely embroidered in a darker shade. Her hat was a picture model of black straw, offset with feathers. Her flowers were a corsage of bride's roses and valley lilies.

Dr. and Mrs. McClendon left immediately for Signal Mountain, Tenn. and later will go to Asheville. After two weeks they will make their home in Goodwater, Ala.

HARTFORD, CI., May 20, 1919.


Labor on the tobacco farms of Con-
necticut is abundant this year. This
condition is greatly in contrast to that
of year ago, when the munition fac
tories were paying high wages to thou
sands of workmen. At that time the
tobacco growers could not get help at
any price, and so the crops suffered in
consequence.


This season many of the men at work
on the tobacco plantations were en-
gagged in the warehouses during the
winter and spring, as sorters and pack
ers, and now are ready for the custom
ary work in the fields. Many of these
men are married, and where it is pos
sible, they make their home on the
plantations nearby, and often times
their children find work there.


Although many of the men who go
to work in the tobacco fields leave in a
short time, yet another force of en-
ployes comes along, so that the tobacco
plantation employer does not suffer for
lack of help.

Chicago, May 25.—President Wilson's candidacy for third term will be determined largely by the fate of the League of Nations, in the opinion of Homer S. Cummings, chairman of the Democratic National Committee, who came to Chicago today to preside at two days' session of that body.

"While I have no information regarding President Wilson's intentions about becoming a candidate for third term, I believe that the question largely rests on the fate of the League of Nations," said Chairman Cummings. "If the League of Nations should by any chance be defeated, and this to my mind is unthinkable, the pressure brought to bear on the President to run again would be very great and I feel certain that he would be re-elected. If the League of Nations is successful I do not think the pressure would be nearly as great."

In the absence of definite word from President Wilson on the subject there was little gossip of candidates among the party leaders. The names most frequently mentioned were William G. McAdoo, former secretary of the treasury and A. Mitchell Palmer, United States attorney general, who will address the committee tomorrow night.

Every state was represented by either committeeman or proxy when Chairman Cummings called the body to order in session which formally marks the opening of the presidential campaign of 1920.

Reactionaries Leading Republicans

Chairman Cummings praised the record of progressive achievements of the Democratic National administration and declared that the Republican party again is falling under reactionary leadership as indicated by the recent organization of Congress.

He urged a closer co-operation between the different departments of the party organization in preparing for the next national campaign and referred to the important part women will take in future political activities.

He said he expected to visit every state in the union before returning to New York in August. Party headquarters, he added, would remain in Washington until the opening of the 1920 campaign, when they would be removed to New York. It was probable that sub headquarters would be opened in Chicago and perhaps other cities later. In a few days Mr. Cummings will appoint a number of committees to take up active work for the next president's campaign.

London, July 24.—With the subscription
lists opened on June 10 and closing on
July 11, the offering of the "Victory
Loan" has been the event of the past
month in British finance.

The Government's new loan for an un-
limited amount has taken two terms
with alternative attractions for differ-
ent classes of investors, but its single
object, that of funding as much as pos-
sible of the outstanding "Floating" and
early-maturing short-dated debt raised
during the war. Apart from its own in-
herent recommendations to the subscrip-
ters, strong appeal has been made to
the nation to invest in it, as a matter
of patriotic duty, in order that by this
funding, the London money market may
be freed from the continuous demands
of the Exchequer for renewing its short
borrowings, and thus made able to devote
its resources to the financing of trade
and industry, while at the same time a
great step will have been taken to re-
store stable currency position by the
reduction of inflation. The issue has
been a great success.

One of the two securities offered is
termed Funding Loan. It is four
per cent stock convertible into bonds at
the holders' option, issued at 80, and re-
deemable at par (100) not earlier than the
year 1880 nor later than 1890. With a
clear interest yield of 5 per cent, it is
thus an ideal long-dated investment of
the trustee type. It has a sinking fund
of half of one per cent per annum on
the total issue attached to it; and the
stock will be accepted at its subscrip-
tion price of 80 per cent as cash for
payment of death duties to the govern-
ment on the estate entries of original
subscribers or of holders for six months
immediately preceding death. Dividends
are paid half yearly on May 1, and No-
vember 1.

The other issue is in the form of Lib-
erty Bonds. These are four per cent,
sold at subscription price of $85 for
each $100 bond, redeemable by annual
drawings at par (100) between Septem-
ber 1, 1920, and September 1, 1876. Their
interest yield over the full period of 56
years thus works out at about 4.25 per
cent, but of course, the return to the
investor is higher according as the re-
demption by annual drawings comes ear-
lier. Thus on bonds drawn in the first
year 1920 the original subscriber really
gets return of 5.25 per cent; in 1921
4.10 per cent; in 1922 4.07 per cent;
and so on, to 3.30 per cent if his bonds
are drawn in 1893, 3.50 per cent if in
also in 1899. To secure the final re-
demption by annual drawings in 56 years
a sinking fund of half of one per cent
per annum is provided. Dividends are paid
half yearly on March 1 and September 1.
The VICTORY Bonds will be accepted as
cash payment of death duties not at their
subscription price as in the case of the
Funding Loan, but at their face value,
i.e., as $100 for each $85 paid bond, a
specially valuable point.

Apart from cash subscriptions both
forms of loan have been offered to the
holders of British Government Treasury
Bills, which could be converted into them
under discount at 2.25 per cent, or of the
following short dated Government Se-
curities, convertible at par: the 4.25 per
cent War loan 1920, 1921, and 1927, 4
per cent Exchequer Bonds 1921 and
1927, and 4 per cent National War Puts of
the LIST, End and Bird series—includ-
ing only the last series—War Bonds
dated from February 1, 1871.

Samuel Gompers, president of the American Federation of Labor, Warren I. Stone, chief of the engineers brotherhood, and Glenn F. Plumb, author of organized labor's solution of the railroad problem and general counsel for the railroad brotherhoods, in turn presented varying arguments, but all emphasizing the single point that in their view no power could constitutionally prevent men from leaving work at their will.

"I do not wish to live a single day after that right has been taken away from working men," Mr. Gompers said with more than a touch of indignation. He served notice on the committee that the anti-strike provision, if enacted as law, would not be obeyed.

"With a full sense of my responsibility," he told senators, "I say that I should have no more hesitancy about participating in strike after its passage than I do now. It would not stop strikes; it would just make law breakers."

There was considerable reference to the Plumb plan, which provides for government ownership of the railroads and joint operation by the public and employees, when its author opened his statement. He declared that strikes would be beneficial in the future, because workers would use them to force down prices instead of merely to secure a greater share of the cost of production, and allowing prices to increase. Puzzled senatorial questioners dealt at some length with this theory, but did not share his conclusion.

Likewise Mr. Plumb made reference to approaching revolution should "conservative labor forces" not secure concessions of the type embodied in his plan and this occasioned more querying. Mr. Stone attacked the Cummins bill in its entirety. Its committee on wages and working conditions, he said, was a mere bluff; it cinchéd bureaucratic control on the roads; it distorted the structure of the Interstate Commerce Commission in order to give the committee a mandate to fix rates on the basis of inflated capitalization and had a transportation board just to take the blame off the guilty railroad officials for denying rights to labor.

Broad St. He delivered a ringing address, commanding the good work of his deputy Grand Master for this district and several worshipful masters of the lodges of the city, who also briefly addressed the lodge. M., when the distinguished guest and his party left for the south, being at Charlotte, N. C. on Sunday and Monday the 10th and 11th instants. Many candidates were initiated and many were present from all over the state, and many were present at the banquet. The official program shown tells of it in a most prosperous condition both financially and numerically. Six Nobles died during 1918, two hundred and eighty-five Nobles, the service of which I've mentioned, sum Major, twenty-sixty-four Lieutenants, forty-two Lieutenants, and one hundred and three non-commissioned officers and privates, one lieutenant having died at Quantico on Jan. 1st, 1912. The total membership of Acca Temple was 1,354, and they hope to soon make it 1,500.

St. Andrew's Lodge, No. 1, Knight Templar, held its asylum in Masonic Temple, 100 W. Broad street, last night; the 10th instant, much business was transacted and an evening meeting held.

The first annual communication of the Grand Lodge, Va. and N. J., met in Masonic Temple, 100 W. Broad Street, last Tuesday night. Ernest Lee Cunningham, most worshipful Grand Master, of Newport News, has been in the city for several days presiding. The Grand Master's report was a very elaborate one and showed a large increase in membership. Three sessions a day were held, the final one being Lodge members and visiting brothers. They retired to the banquet hall, when a sumptuous feast was enjoyed. About 400 representatives and visitors attended the annual communication, entertaining many of Virginia's most prominent citizens. The menu prepared by the committee was very fine. The Masonic Temple, 100 W. Broad street, has for the past week been in the hands of the Grand Lodge. Many delegates took opportunity to visit homes near the city and look after its welfare.

But in the spring step of youth, so George Washington Moody came to the city from Surry county to add a touch of youthful buoyancy to the crowd, and attended performances of the Grand Lodge of Masons, who met here last Tuesday in annual conciave.

Mr. Moody has been climbing the mountain of life for eighty-five years, but is well on the sunny side of life. The remarks at Valley Forge were from old friends of his, yet only his strict regard for truth kept the district of Surry from handing him a suit of olive drab.

Sixty-four years ago, long before the time of the J. W. and the secessionists, he became master Mason in Jefferson Lodge, Surry county. For over half a century he has been active in the lodge.
